title: Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the European College of Sport Science and the American College of Sports Medicine
authors: Meeusen R, Duclos M, Foster C, Fry A, Gleeson M, Nieman D, Raglin J, Rietjens G, Steinacker J, Urhausen A
population: Athletes in general (consensus statement, not a study population)
findings: Functional overreaching is a short-term performance decrement without severe psychological or lasting negative symptoms that leads to improved performance after recovery.

When athletes do not respect the balance between training and recovery, nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR) can occur; distinguishing NFOR from overtraining syndrome (OTS) is very difficult, depends on clinical outcome and exclusion diagnosis, and athletes often show the same clinical, hormonal and other signs and symptoms.
A keyword in recognising OTS is 'prolonged maladaptation' of the athlete and of several biological, neurochemical and hormonal regulation mechanisms.
It is generally thought OTS symptoms (fatigue, performance decline, mood disturbance) are more severe than NFOR, but there is no scientific evidence to confirm or refute this.

Diagnosis involves excluding organic disease or infection, caloric restriction (negative energy balance), insufficient carbohydrate and/or protein intake, iron deficiency, magnesium deficiency, allergies, and identifying initiating events or triggers.
Several markers (hormones, performance tests, psychological tests, biochemical and immune markers) are used, but none meets all the criteria for generally accepted use.

Functional overreaching causes a short-term performance decrement and leads to improved performance after recovery; non-functional overreaching (NFOR) can occur when the balance between training and recovery is not respected.
Distinguishing NFOR from overtraining syndrome (OTS) is very difficult and depends on clinical outcome and exclusion diagnosis; 'prolonged maladaptation' is the keyword.

Etiology work involves excluding organic disease or infection, caloric restriction, insufficient carbohydrate and/or protein, iron deficiency, magnesium deficiency, allergies and others, plus identifying triggers.
Several markers (hormones, performance tests, psychological, biochemical, immune) are used, but none meet all the criteria for generally accepted use.
limitations: Expert consensus; offers no validated numeric thresholds a wearable app could apply. Evidence for markers is explicitly insufficient.
implications: Model overreaching risk as a flag with a conservative response (reduce load, schedule recovery); never output an OTS diagnosis.
When a flag persists, show a prompt to see a clinician and to consider illness, under-fuelling (energy availability), and iron status.
No numeric thresholds are justified by this paper; any thresholds the engine uses are design choices (grade D).
No single biomarker (including HRV or resting HR) can diagnose overreaching; flags should prompt load reduction, not diagnoses.
Persistent unexplained performance decline and fatigue or mood change should trigger a rest/deload suggestion and a prompt to see a clinician; the duration threshold is not given by the source.
Plan copy should prompt checks of energy intake, iron status, illness and sleep before attributing fatigue to training.

verification.notes: Crossref gives title without the 'joint consensus statement' subtitle, MSSE, 2013, no author list; PubMed gives full title, authors, vol 45(1):186-205. Findings re-checked against the PubMed abstract; added the statement that OTS-more-severe-than-NFOR is unproven.
